quotes.text: The testimony showed that he was the owner of the house, and had leased it to Mitchell for a term without any knowledge or intent that it would be unlawfully used1 by the lessee. By his contract, he parted with all control over it for the term.
Section 2 of the act confers on the lessor of property the power to avoid his contract of lease for the cause named; but it does not make the omission to exercise the power an indictable offense.
the accused rented the house in question, of which he was the owner, to Mitchell for the term of one year, at the rate of $50 per month

new: An owner who leased his house in good faith for a year, without knowledge of illegal use, is not criminally liable under the house-of-ill-fame statute merely for refusing to avoid the lease and re-enter after learning the tenant used it for prostitution. Having leased, he parted with control for the term; the statutory power to avoid the lease imposed no duty to exercise it.
reader: Letting for a year, not short-term, but bears on owner's freedom to let and limits of regulation of lessors.

quotes.text: If the original verbal contract of lease was for a term of seven months only, and the tenant holds over and the landlord elects to treat him as a tenant, such tenant cannot be held for the period of a year, but only for seven months, the length of the original term.
Where the letting is by the day, week, month, or quarter, at a specific rent for the specific term, the letting is a daily, weekly, monthly or quarterly tenancy, according to the circumstances.
A parol contract for a lease between landlord and tenant, and the tenant in possession under a prior verbal lease, is within the statute of frauds and void
he entered into a contract with defendant to lease to her certain premises, at the rate of $30 per month, from the 1st of December, 1896, until the 1st day of July, 1897

new: A parol lease made while the tenant is already in possession is void under the statute of frauds absent a new taking of possession. Where the original letting of the house was for seven months at $30 per month, a holdover tenant can be held only for a like seven-month term, not a year, so the directed verdict for the landlord's extra month's rent was reversed.
reader: Short-period letting of a dwelling by month; owner's claim for further rent defeated, hence adverse. owner_freedom_characterization not addressed by the court.

quotes.text: The debtor did not lose his right to have the homestead set off to him, by leasing the premises for the year, and going, with his family, to another county for temporary purposes.
leased the same, by a written agreement, for one year, and went with his family to another county of the state for temporary purposes

new: A debtor who leased his house and lot for a year and went with his family to another county for temporary purposes did not thereby lose his right to have the premises set off as a homestead exempt from execution. Once regularly set off, no further proceedings could be had against the homestead.
reader: Letting one's dwelling for pay treated as consistent with retaining homestead rights; term was a year, so not short-term.

quotes.text: The statutory notice to leave the premises, required to be given in an action of forcible entry against a tenant holding over his term, may be served as well before as after the expiration of the term.

new: In forcible detainer against a tenant holding over, the statutory three days' notice to leave may be served before the expiration of the term, and the justice need not render judgment immediately upon the verdict.
reader: Procedural landlord-tenant case; favorable only in easing the owner's recovery of possession. owner_freedom left null for want of a supporting passage.

quotes.text: The right of a widow to remain in the mansion house of her deceased husband, as provided by statute, is not restricted, to a personal continuance in the house merely, but she is entitled to a reasonable enjoyment of the possession of the premises, and may therefore either personally occupy .them or she may rent them, as she may deem best promotive of her comfort.

it would be an unreasonable limitation' to restrict it to a right of personal continuance in the mansion-house merely, and deny to her such reasonable enjoyment of the possession of the premises, as she may deem promotive of her comfort.
it may be that she could only derive her support from the premises by renting them
The plaintiff’s dower in said lot and the real estate of said decedent was assigned to her, as of the rents and profits thereof, on the 25th day of November, 1870.

new: A widow entitled by statute to remain in her deceased husband's mansion house until dower is assigned is not confined to personal occupancy: she may instead rent the premises as she deems best for her comfort. Where the administrator instead rented the house and collected the rents, she may recover those rents from him in his representative capacity.
reader: Occupancy period at issue ran months (March to November 1870); letting by a householder-widow treated as within her right of possession.

quotes.text: An entry under a lease for a term of years at an annual rent, void for any cause, and payment of rent under it, creates a tenancy from year to year upon the terms of the lease, except as to its duration.

the plaintiff in error became a tenant for that year upon the terms of the former occupancy, and was not relieved from its obligation to pay the rent for the balance of the year by the abandonment of the premises

new: Entry under an unacknowledged lease for years with payment of rent creates a tenancy from year to year on the lease's terms; a tenant holding over and paying rent into a new year is bound for that year's rent and cannot end the tenancy without the landlord's consent.
reader: Commercial premises; favorable in enforcing the letting on the owner's terms. owner_freedom left null for want of an express passage.

quotes.text: Notice to quit is not necessary to terminate a tenancy from year to year arising from the tenant holding over his term.
the landlord has the option to treat him as a tenant for another year, or as a trespasser

new: No six months' notice to quit is needed to end a year-to-year tenancy arising from holding over; the landlord may treat the holdover as a tenant for another year or as a trespasser and recover possession after the statutory three days' notice. A parol agreement for a future ten-year lease with a tenant in possession is within the statute of frauds.
reader: Store room let by owner's heirs; outcome favors the owner's control over the letting. owner_freedom left null for want of a supporting passage.

quotes.text: It appeared by the affidavit filed with the justice that the defendants, in May, 1885, leased to the prosecutor a seaside cottage and appurtenances, at the city of Cape May, for five years; that at the expiration of that period the lease was continued for an additional five years,

The justice having had jurisdiction of the proceedings before him, the certiorari must be dismissed, with costs.

new: Lessors of a Cape May seaside cottage under a five-year lease (twice renewed on the same terms) validly terminated it on six months' notice under a reserved termination privilege, which was held to be one of the 'terms' carried into the renewals. No second notice under the lease or the Landlord and Tenant act was required, so the justice had jurisdiction of the summary removal proceeding and the certiorari was dismissed.

reader: Long-term lease of a resort cottage; favorable only in that the lessor's contractual right to end the letting on its own terms was enforced. Owner's liberty to let not framed; marginal relevance.

quotes.text: On demise of a house or lands, there is no contract or condition-implied that the premises shall be fit and suitable for the use for which the lessee requires them.
one George Clyne was the lessee and tenant of said house, and hired the same of the defendant

new: On the demise of a house there is no implied condition that it is fit for use; the landlord owes no duty of repair to the tenant's sister living as a member of his family, who is neither in privity of estate nor of contract, so the declaration was bad on demurrer.
reader: Tenancy of a dwelling-house of indefinite, evidently long duration.

quotes.text: That the said M. Elizabeth Lucas, tenant in common as aforesaid, does hereby let unto William Neil, of the city of Philadelphia, for the term of four months from the lstday of June, a. d. 1895, the said premises known as the Beach House, situate at Sea Girt, New Jersey, consisting of a hotel fully furnished

but to create between those persons the relation of lessor and lessee, and to secure to Mrs. Lucas her stipulated share of the net receipts of the business which Mr. Neil was to carry on in the hotel, not as profits due to a partner, but as rent due to a lessor.

new: A four-month letting of a furnished summer hotel, at a rent measured by a share of the hotel's surplus receipts and with supervisory safeguards for the lessor, was held to be a lease and not a partnership. The lessor was therefore not liable to creditors of the hotel business.
reader: Letting of a hotel to an operator; owner's freedom to let on her own terms upheld.

the resolutions of council granting the licenses, and the licenses themselves, are all without jurisdiction and void

new: Licenses to keep inns and taverns in Atlantic City were set aside because the statutory recommendations were not genuinely signed by twelve reputable freeholders. The court treated inn and tavern keeping as an activity that may be pursued only under a license granted on strict statutory conditions.

This decision has long remained unquestioned, and the point decided must be considered res judicata.

reader: Marginal: procedural summary-dispossess case on a monthly tenancy; nature of premises and landlord not stated. Favorable only in that the landlord's remedy to recover possession was upheld.

quotes.text: it is undoubtedly the law, that the landlord becomes responsible for the maintenance of a disorderly house by his tenant, if he has rented the establishment to the tenant to be kept as ;a disorderly house, or with the anticipation upon his part that :it would be so kept.

There is nothing there to indicate that they did not receive their rights daily, and if they received their rights daily, paying for them daily, what is ■there to indicate that the owners of the property, the Engemans, are not the landlords for whom Mr. Primrose is collecting the daily rent?

new: Owners of a race track who daily let booths to bookmakers with knowledge of the illegal betting were properly convicted of keeping a disorderly house; a landlord who lets premises anticipating disorderly use is responsible for its maintenance.
reader: Daily lettings of booths, not dwelling rooms.

quotes.text: The agreement shows their relation to-have been that of master and servant, and not of landlord and tenant.
his removal could be accomplished by the act of the owner, without the aid of any judicial tribunal.

the plaintiff, McQuade, was employed by the defendant, Emmons, by the month; that as compensation for the services to be rendered by Mc-Quade, he was to receive from the defendant $25 a month, and the use of a house for himself and his family

new: A workman occupying his employer's tenement house as part of his wages is not a tenant but a servant; the occupancy ends with the service and the owner may remove him without judicial process, so landlord-and-tenant removal proceedings gave the justice no jurisdiction.

quotes.text: There is nothing illegal in an agreement to transfer a license to keep an inn, although the license after its transfer will be inoperative.
The defendant agreed to give $2000, in consideration of the assignment of a certain lease, and the sale and transfer to him of certain personal property.

new: An agreement to transfer an inn license along with a lease and chattels is not illegal, though the license itself becomes inoperative on transfer; the assignee could not be required to accept an assignment enlarging his covenants, and the vendor who resold the premises could not sue on the deposit check.
reader: Statute makes the inn license non-transferable (adverse element) while upholding the private bargain (favorable element).

quotes.text: The plaintiff leased to Henry W. Abbott, the Lake House,, at Spring Lake Beach, Monmouth county, for the term of one year from the 1st day of April, 1879, at the yearly rent of $1000,

A mere breach of covenant by the tenant, such as the non-payment of rent at the time appointed, gives the landlord no right of entry, unless there be a stipulation in the lease that such breach of covenant shall work a forfeiture and determination of the tenant’s interest.
Bui the eviction, to have the effect of suspending the rent, must be effected before the rent becomes due, for the rent 'already accrued and overdue is not forfeited by the eviction.

new: Landlord who refused the tenant of the Lake House re-entry unless overdue rent was paid evicted him; absent a re-entry stipulation non-payment gives no right of entry, and eviction suspends rent going forward. But rent already accrued before the eviction is not forfeited, so the sureties remained liable for the September instalment; recoupment is unavailable in covenant on a sealed lease.

reader: One-year lease of a resort house (Lake House). Mixed: landlord's self-help re-entry condemned as eviction (adverse, common-law limit on owner), but accrued rent preserved (favorable). Owner's liberty to let not discussed.

quotes.text: the council may limit the exercise of those rights if they deem such limitation expedient for the peace and good order of the borough

For the reasons that the ordinance was not introduced at a previous meeting, and because the penalty is without legal authority, the second section of the ordinance, which has been enforced against the prosecutors, will be set aside, without costs.
such ordinance would be unreasonably restrictive in cities or thoroughfares where public travel demands that places be kept open for refreshment at later hours

new: The borough could, under its power to preserve peace and good order, ordain a ten o'clock closing hour binding on licensed inns and taverns, but this particular ordinance was set aside because it was not introduced at a previous meeting and because it added forfeiture of license to the fine without charter authority.
reader: Police power over licensed inns affirmed in principle; the specific ordinance annulled.

quotes.text: the tenancy being a monthly one, at $8 per month, payable in advance
The acts of the landlord and those who represented him did not constitute a trespass; the surrender of the premises by the tenant must, in law, be regarded as voluntary

new: A monthly tenant who left after a mere threat of future removal, before any warrant to dispossess was delivered, surrendered voluntarily; the landlord therefore committed no trespass and the judgment against him was reversed.
reader: Monthly letting of a dwelling; landlord's recovery of possession upheld against tenant's trespass action.

quotes.text: The order of the Court of Common Pleas granting the license, and the license granted, are vacated, without costs.
the sole and exclusive power to grant licenses to persons to keep inns and taverns within said town, was vested in the common council.

new: The 1879 supplement transferring inn and tavern licensing to the Common Pleas was an unconstitutional local law, so the Common Pleas license to keep an inn and tavern in Lambertville was vacated and the town council's exclusive licensing power remained.

quotes.text: the license which it granted to the applicant to keep an inn and tavern in the house where he then dwelt

However binding they may be upon the parties to such instruments, they are in no wise obligatory upon the court in the exercise of its statutory discretion to grant licenses for the public convenience, nor can such provisions render licenses granted invalid.
its exercise is made by the statute discretionary in that court

new: The Common Pleas had jurisdiction to license Busby to keep an inn and tavern in the house where he dwelt, its discretion is not reviewable on certiorari, and private deed covenants against selling liquor do not restrain the court from granting a license for the public convenience.
reader: Householder licensed to keep an inn in his own dwelling; challenge to the license dismissed, so favorable to the keeper's right to entertain for pay.

quotes.text: Prosecutors hold their property and their right to sell it subject to the police power of this municipality, which may reasonably restrict an injurious use of it detrimental to good order.
each of the prosecutors was licensed by the common council of the borough to keep an inn or tavern therein
travelers arriving there by the last evening train reach the inns of prosecutors a little before ten o’clock

new: A borough ordinance closing the bars of licensed inns and taverns between ten at night and four in the morning was a reasonable exercise of the power to preserve peace and good order, notwithstanding pre-existing licenses and loss of profits.
reader: Regulation of licensed inns/taverns; occupancy duration inferred from traveler use.

quotes.text: The ordinances of Jersey City provide that no person licensed to keep an inn and tavern in the city shall expose intoxicating liquors for sale on Sunday.
I cannot suppose that this was an exposure of intoxicating liquors for sale within the meaning of the ordinance.

new: An inn and tavern keeper's mere keeping of liquor in its usual place in the bar on Sunday was not an 'exposure for sale' violating the city ordinance, and the conviction was reversed; the city's power to license and regulate innkeepers was assumed throughout.
reader: Occupancy duration of guests not discussed.

quotes.text: The complainant owns the adjoining lot, the house upon which is, and has been for years, occupied by her as a dwelling-house and boarding-house. It is kept as a boarding-house of the first class, and the complainant has a great many guests who regularly stay at her house.

The title of the complainant to her premises, and to be protected from injury in the prosecution of a valuable and lawful business, is clear and is not disputed. If the injury was certain, or without reasonable doubt, I should not hesitate to grant the injunction.

That such an establishment beside her house, even if it did not by the smoke and noise render life uncomfortable, would injure the prestige of her house, make it less desirable for that bettor class of boarders who frequent it, and thus lessen her profits, is no good ground for restraining the defendants.

And many localities, which were the residence of the most refined and cultivated, have been deserted by them, because persons who pursue_ the occupation of the complainant have opened boarding-houses in them. Yet in these cases the damage results from lawful acts, and in equity as well as at law, there is no remedy for damnum absque injuria.

new: A first-class boarding-house keeper sought to enjoin construction of an adjacent steam planing mill as a nuisance. The court treated her boarding-house as a valuable and lawful business entitled to protection from actual nuisance, but refused the injunction because the nuisance was not yet shown beyond doubt; loss of prestige or of a better class of boarders from lawful neighboring uses is damnum absque injuria. In passing the court remarked that boarding-houses themselves make refined neighborhoods undesirable.

reader: Keeper resides in the house but runs it as a first-class enterprise with many guests, so coded commercial_operator. Duration of guests' stays not stated ('regularly stay'). Favorable on the holding (boarding-house is lawful business protected from nuisance); adverse-flavored dictum that boarding-houses degrade refined neighborhoods, noted as tension.

quotes.text: A widow, whose dower has not been assigned, cannot be required to account for the rent of the mansion-house, although she has rented it and received rent for it. Her tenant’s possession is hers.
Nor is it liable to forfeiture by reason of the failure of the widow to occupy in person. She may occupy by her tenant.
For part of the time since her husband’s death, she has rented the premises and received the rent.

new: A widow entitled to quarantine in the mansion-house may let it to a tenant and keep the rent without accounting to the heirs; her tenant's possession is her own occupancy.

appellant not only collects the rentals but also provides managerial, janitorial, and other services for the tenants

quotes.text: We conclude that the Housing Authority is entitled to judgment in ejectment in this case and that appellant-tenant has not been denied due process or deprived of any constitutional right.

quotes.text: On September 24, 1942, the Fidelity-Philadelphia Trust Company, Trustee, then owner of premises No. 120 St. Paul’s Road, Ardmore, entered into a written lease of that property with the defendant for a term of one year from October 15,1942, at an annual rent of $780.00, payable at the rate of $65.00 per month.

Appellant contends also that the acceptance by the landlords of rent after the expiration of the time set forth in the notice to quit constitutes a waiver of the notice, but with that contention we do not agree.

quotes.text: The landlord, having the right to reenter and repossess premises for default in rents by the terms of the lease, had implied authority to remove furniture or other property from the demised premises and. place it in storage or elsewhere at the owner’s risk.

quotes.text: It cannot reasonably be conceived that the Act was intended to embrace the hotelkeeper who dispenses such articles primarily to his guests on the premises, thereby serving their convenience as a part of his recognized obligation to care for their comfort. quotes.text: In the absence of anything to show the contrary, the letting of an apartment in an apartment building carries with it a right of way, appurtenant to the apartment and available to the tenant, his family, guests and invitees, in the common doorways, corridors, stairways and the like that afford access to the apartment.

This was a license for the tenants to grant or withhold, one embraced within the easement conferred upon them by the letting, one which subsisted until revoked by the tenants, and one which the tenants could exercise notwithstanding objections of the landlord, who could not revoke the license any more than he could an invitation extended by the tenant to one calling upon any legitimate business.
Aysies testified, however, that he did not live in the building.

Aysies testified that he built the apartment house in 1925 and that at that time the tenants requested that no pedlers or solicitors be allowed and that that was a rule, but that none of the original tenants was in occupancy on July 13, 1942, and that none of the tenants then in occupancy had made any such request.

new: Letting an apartment carries an appurtenant easement over common corridors for the tenant and the tenant's guests, invitees and licensees. Jehovah's Witnesses admitted by tenants through the buzzer system were licensees of the tenants, and the non-resident landlord could not revoke that license; trespass convictions reversed.

reader: Adverse only in the sense that tenant rights in common areas override the owner's control; the owner's right to let itself was not questioned. Duration inferred from ordinary apartment tenancies (rule dating from 1925); owner_freedom_characterization is not_addressed.

quotes.text: If a tenant at will in a dwelling fails to pay his rent and there is served upon him a fourteen days’ notice to quit under G. L. (Ter. Ed.) c. 186, § 12, he becomes a tenant at sufferance at the expiration of the fourteen day period, and a member of his household cannot recover from the landlord for injuries thereafter sustained by reason of a defect in a stairway maintained by the landlord for the use of the tenant if such injuries are not caused by wilful, wanton or reckless conduct on the part of the landlord.
A tenant at sufferance is a bare licensee to whom the landlord owes merely the duty not wantonly nor wilfully to injure him.

The answer to this statement is that under our statute a tenant at will who has received a fourteen days’ notice to quit for nonpayment of rent cannot by paying the rent in full revive the tenancy, and a fortiori, a tenant who not only has received a notice to quit for nonpayment, but upon whom summary process has already been served, cannot revive the tenancy.

new: A residential tenant at will who fails to pay rent and receives a fourteen days' notice to quit becomes a tenant at sufferance—a bare licensee—on expiry of the notice, and cannot revive the tenancy by tendering rent. The landlord thereafter owes the tenant's household only a duty not to injure wantonly or wilfully, so no recovery for a defective stairway.

reader: Favorable in that the owner's termination of a residential tenancy at will on his own terms was enforced against the occupant; the court did not frame the right to let generally (owner_freedom not_addressed). Residence status of landlord not stated; coded non_resident_owner as house 'owned and controlled by the defendant' with tenants in occupancy.

Whenever a tenancy at will of premises occupied for dwelling purposes, other than a room or rooms in a hotel, lodging house or rooming house is terminated, without fault of the tenant, either by operation of law or by act of the landlord except as provided in section twelve, no action to recover possession of the premises shall be brought, nor shall the tenant be dispossessed, until after the expiration of a period, equal to the interval between the days on which the rent reserved is payable, from the time when the tenant receives notice in writing of such termination;

new: A purchaser of a dwelling house occupied by a monthly tenant at will could not maintain summary process: G.L. c. 186 § 13 barred an action until a full rent interval after written notice of termination, and a landlord has no right to enter to inspect absent agreement, so a notice to quit resting on refusal of inspection was ineffective. The court noted the statute's exclusion of rooms in hotels, lodging houses and rooming houses.

reader: Adverse: statutory tenant protection and no implied right of landlord entry defeat the owner's recovery of possession. Notable for the statutory carve-out of hotel/lodging-house/rooming-house rooms from the notice protection, which implies lodgers are treated differently from dwelling tenants. reader: Marginal: householder letting an apartment in own house; duration of tenancy not stated. Adverse only in the weak sense of a duty imposed on the letting owner.

I, §26 (guaranteeing an owner's absolute discretion to decline to sell, lease or rent residential property) unconstitutional in its entirety, so a redevelopment agency could accept federal anti-discrimination conditions. agreed to rent to him suite No. five (5) in the ‘Helberta’ apartment house, as a place of residence for himself and family, for the term of six months for the sum of one hundred and thirty-two ($132) dollars
